The docs show a per-caller token exchange in clientFor, and say that forwarding the same token is correct only when one authorization server issued it for both audiences. Nothing in the package makes passthrough the easy path.

@summationai/axe-mcp is a resource server, not an authorization server. It verifies tokens through the SDK's OAuthTokenVerifier interface, answers 401 and 403 with WWW-Authenticate (resource_metadata, scope), and builds the RFC 9728 document. The SDK's own bearer middleware and metadata router are Express-only; the Web-standard handler reimplements the same responses in a few lines instead of pulling Express into a package that runs on Workers.

Freshness is a bound plus two triggers, not a poll loop. A remote manifest is revalidated when it is older than the smaller of manifestMaxAgeMs and the site's max-age, when a tool call names a tool the copy lacks, and after not_found. Revalidation is a conditional request, so an ETag on the manifest (added to @summationai/axe-core) makes the eager setting cheap. There is no background timer in the package; refresh() exists for hosts that want one, as the docs show. Notifications compare the derived tool list, not the manifest, so a new live.rev does not send tools/list_changed.

Retry identity is an optional idempotencyKey argument, not deduplication by input. Two calls with identical arguments may be two intended orders, so the bridge never infers a retry from matching inputs: without a key every call gets a fresh one. With a key the site's operation claim ([P-OP-1]) already gives the right answers (stored envelope, in_progress, conflict for different input), so recovery is repeating the call, and no separate status tool was added. The argument reuses the envelope field's name so there is one word for one idea.

Limits and schema boundaries (review 2026-09-24, item 12)

An oversized body is invalid_input with a reason, not a new error code. The error codes are a closed list that every agent switches on ([P-ERR-1]); a tenth code would reach agents built against nine as an unknown value. invalid_input is already what the agent must fix before retrying, retryable: false says not to repeat it, and details.reason: "payload_too_large" follows the precedent of json_required on unsupported. The HTTP status is 413 rather than the mapped 400, because proxies, load balancers, and logs already understand 413; agents decide by the body ([P-INV-7]), so the exception to [P-INV-6] costs them nothing.

1 MiB by default, even though document.base64 allows 10 MiB. Every site pays for the body limit; few accept inline documents. A default sized for the largest kind would let any anonymous caller make every site buffer 14 MiB per request. Sites that take inline documents raise maxBodyBytes, and the kind registry says so; everything else uses document.url.

Nesting is capped at 64 levels, fixed. A 400 KB body of nested arrays overflowed the stack in the canonical JSON hash before any schema ran. No real request envelope needs more than a handful of levels; a configurable limit would be a knob nobody should turn.

The in-memory stores sweep on writes and run no timer. A background timer would need unref, a lifecycle, and a way to stop it in tests, and it would still only matter for a process that writes nothing (whose map is not growing). Sweeping at most once per sweepIntervalMs on a write bounds the cost and the memory with none of that; close() exists to release memory, not to stop anything. maxEntries evicts oldest first but never a claim whose lease is running, because evicting one would let the operation run twice; a store full of running claims throws, which surfaces as a failed request rather than a duplicate charge.

The fingerprint is input as sent. Phase 1 hashed the parsed input. With a transform to a Date, every input hashed the same ({}), so a reused key with a different date replayed the first result; a BigInt would have thrown. The raw input is always JSON (it came from JSON.parse), and the retry of an action that no longer exists could only ever be matched on it. The cost is that two bodies the schema would parse identically (one spelling out a default) are different operations under one key, which an agent resending its own body never hits.

The validator fails closed; it is not Ajv. Measured with esbuild for the browser: the in-house validator is 10 kB minified (3.6 kB gzipped); Ajv 8's draft 2020-12 entry is 134 kB (40 kB), 148 kB (44 kB) with ajv-formats. It ships in @summationai/axe-surface's browser entry (held under 50 kB, no Zod), and Ajv compiles schemas with new Function, which strict CSPs and Cloudflare Workers refuse. Instead of growing toward full JSON Schema, the subset covers what Zod emits and the kinds use, implements the cheap remaining 2020-12 keywords, and refuses the value for anything else: a keyword it does not know, a format it cannot check without a pattern, a pattern that does not compile, an unresolvable or non-local $ref, a $ref loop that consumes nothing. Ignoring any of those would accept what the author meant to refuse. schemaProblems and the lint report the same constructs at build time, so a refusal in production is a lint warning somebody ignored.

Unknown formats pass when a pattern carries them. Zod emits a pattern next to almost every format it writes (cuid2, e164, emoji, starts_with in an allOf), and the pattern is the check. Refusing those formats would break continuation payloads built from ordinary Zod schemas; accepting any format with no pattern would silently widen. So a format is accepted only when the validator checks it or a pattern in the same schema does.

Refinements are marked in the manifest and linted, not rejected. A .refine cannot be written in JSON Schema, and rejecting refined schemas at registration would forbid ordinary validation (a weekday, a date after another). Publishing the looser schema without saying so would tell agents a value is valid when the server will refuse it. x-axe-refined: true on the node is standard JSON Schema (an annotation), costs nothing to agents that ignore it, and lets an agent expect invalid_input; the refined-schema lint warning makes the author decide whether the description explains the rule. Transforms and defaults are not marked, since they change what the handler receives, not what the agent may send; coercion makes the server more permissive than its schema, which is safe.

The backtracking check is a heuristic lint warning. Deciding whether a regular expression backtracks catastrophically needs an automaton analysis this package should not carry. The shape behind nearly every real incident, a repeated group whose body ends in an unbounded repetition, is cheap to recognize, and none of Zod's built-in patterns match it. It warns rather than refuses because false positives are possible and the pattern is the site's own.

The client checks documents by hand, not with the core Zod schemas. Validating with @summationai/axe-core/schemas would pull Zod into @summationai/axe-client, which is dependency-free and was 12 kB. The hand checks cover the members the client and present read, per status, and fail with an AXEClientError naming the member. With timeouts, bounded reads, and polling budgets the entry is 16 kB, so the bundle budget moved from 15 kB to 18 kB.

Client timeouts use a plain timer, not AbortSignal.timeout. One AbortController per call is aborted by the caller's signal or by an unref'd setTimeout, and the timer is cleared when the body finishes. AbortSignal.any is missing from Node 20.0–20.2, and AbortSignal.timeout cannot be cleared early, so a finished request would keep its timer (and, in a short-lived process, keep the process alive until it fired).

Existing agent interfaces (review 2026-09-24, item 14)

WebMCP is a subpath of @summationai/axe-surface, and the provider is its default integration. The adapter needs describeEntry and the Surface type and nothing else; a separate package would depend on @summationai/axe-surface anyway and add a release unit. The main entry and hook-only React imports tree-shake it away, while SurfaceProvider includes it for the webMcp prop. That makes the browser-native path one package and one provider instead of asking every consuming app to wire a second adapter.

Written against the current draft only, behind one indirection. The WebMCP draft moved from navigator.modelContext with provideContext/unregisterTool to document.modelContext with registerTool(tool, { signal }). The adapter implements only the shape the draft and Chrome's documentation state on 2026-09-24, finds it in one function, and registers through another; supporting the older shape would mean implementing an API nobody documents any more.

No tool for a sensitive field, and none for the ledger. A browser agent could type into a PIN field through a tool as easily as through the page, but the point of sensitive is that a person enters it. The ledger can hold typed text under the keep policy; expose still publishes it inside the page for agents that already drive it.

Omitted expectedRev means the current revision. WebMCP agents call tools from the page's own tool list, re-registered as availability changes, so requiring a revision would force an observe round-trip before every click. The surface's availability and confirmation checks still apply, and an agent that planned on an observation can pass its rev to be refused if the page moved.

A WebMCP tool cannot approve its own consequential act. Tool input is agent-controlled, so confirm: true is not a person's consent and exposing handle.approve as another tool would erase the approval boundary. High-risk, explicitly confirmed, and approval-gated calls therefore require an application-supplied requestApproval callback whose UI is outside the tool surface. The adapter records the person's decision and alone reaches the private one-use auto-surface approver; absent, failed, or denied approval refuses the act. This keeps package-only WebMCP viable without weakening the same rule the relay enforces through MCP elicitation.

Tool names use only letters, digits, _, and -. The draft also allows ., but agents hand these tools to model APIs, several of which refuse dots. A colliding id gets a hash of the id, not a counter, so a name never depends on registration order.

Elicitation walks accepts in the site's order and stops at the first sensitive kind. Skipping a preferred sensitive option to put a less preferred one in a form would steer the user away from what the site asked for first. A kind that is not sensitive but has no flat form is skipped, because the model can still supply it. Payment and identity kinds are sensitive for this purpose whatever their flag: MCP forbids payment credentials in forms, and payment.wire-confirmation, though not sensitive in the kind registry, is a payment step that belongs on the site's page.

URL-mode accept is not completion, and login_required is not offered. The bridge cannot know when the user finishes on the site, so it returns the resume token to the model as before rather than waiting. Signing in to the site the bridge speaks for is what MCP authorization is for; the elicitation specification says URL mode must not be used to authorize the user to the server itself.

The Apps view renders the SDK's escaped HTML, delivered in the result's _meta. The view is one static resource that a host may prefetch and cache, so per-call data has to arrive with the result. Rendering toHTML output keeps one renderer; the view parses it with DOMParser (no script runs), removes scripts, handlers, and the affordance buttons, and never evaluates result data. The server declares the resources capability for every client because capabilities are announced before the client's are known; the resource is listed and linked only for hosts that negotiated the extension.

Human oversight and execution modes (review 2026-09-24, items 13 and 15)

An approval is a handoff with bindings, not a new token. Phase 1 already gave the resume token everything an approval must be bound to except the state: the action, the input fingerprint, the principal, the tenant, an expiry, single use through the operation claim, and replay of the stored envelope. A separate approval token would have duplicated that machinery and its tenant and principal checks, and every refusal rule written for it. So requestApproval is a handoff whose token record also keeps the input as sent, the state approvalState reported, and the decision. The agent's side is unchanged: needs_human, a link, /axe/resume.

The runtime computes the bound state; the handler does not pass it. A handler that passed its own state value could pass the wrong one, or one read before a write it then forgot. approvalState is one function the runtime calls at the request, at the approval, and at the resume, so the three comparisons cannot use different definitions. The cost is a small window between the handler reading the state for its preview and the runtime reading it for the binding; the approval page renders the current state from the site's store, and a moved state is refused at approval anyway.

Invalidation is permanent. A state that changed and changed back (an edit undone) would make a stale approval valid again under an equality check alone, after the person has seen a different plan. Once a mismatch is observed, the request is invalidated for good and the agent asks again. With a revision counter the question never arises; with a status or a content value it would.

Approval is recorded by the site's code, never inferred from a request. The SDK cannot see a browser, a session, or a click. approveHandoff takes the approver's name from the site, after the site's own session check, CSRF protection, and authorization. Nothing reaching the AXE endpoints (an input flag, a payload, a resume body) can set it; a test sends confirm: true, approved: true, and approvedBy on the resume and gets handoffStatus: "open". Whether a person may approve their own agent's request is the site's policy; the reference app lets an approver do so and refuses a planner.

Cancel applies to every handoff, and not to committed work. A person who declines a signature request should be able to say so, not wait for expiry, so cancelHandoff works on any unused handoff. A handoff whose resume ran, or is running, answers used: the effect happened, and pretending to cancel it would be worse than refusing. Undo is an action of the site's own; reversible: true describes one and implements nothing.

Decisions are read-modify-write on the TokenStore, like completeHandoff. Making them atomic would need a compare-and-set on TokenStore, a breaking interface change for every store adapter, for a race between two people deciding the same request within milliseconds. The resume re-reads the record after it claims the operation, which closes the common interleaving (a cancel before the resume starts); the handler's conditional write at the bound state is the guarantee against running on changed state. The limit is documented.

Approval events come from the runtime, not the handler. The lifecycle has transitions no handler sees (approval and cancellation happen on the site's page, invalidation inside the runtime). Emitting them as action events on the existing onActionEvent channel gives a site one feed for its history, under the existing rule that action events carry identifiers and actors and never payloads.

Execution modes are a spec section, because the absence of a broker is a property integrators rely on. A reviewer's reading of the React hook plus a Next route suggested one registry; there are two, and nothing connects them. Stating it as [S-MODE-1] to [S-MODE-4] gives WebMCP and other in-page adapters a rule to build against (connect explicitly, state the scope) and tells integrators where shared state must live (the server, behind a conditional write).

The reference app is a workspace package outside the build graph. It depends on Next and React 19, which the SDK packages must not; it has no build script, so pnpm -r build does not run next build, and its Node suite runs in pnpm -r test because it is fast and deterministic. The browser suite needs a production build and Chromium, so it has its own script, the way the site's does. Server state is in memory behind a conditional write that has no await between the check and the write: the same semantics as UPDATE ... WHERE rev = $expected, without adding a database dependency to the repository.

Evaluation (review 2026-09-24, item 17)

Four variants, because the trials' own finding splits the claim in two. The Surface trials attributed two of three gains against browser agents to accessible names alone. Comparing "AXE" with "a browser agent on the page" would have credited the protocol with what the markup bought, so the markup gets its own variant (V2) between the bare page (V1) and the tools. The tools are split the same way: a thin CRUD wrapper (V3) against AXE with live state (V4), so what the revision, availability, approvals, and idempotency add is measured against tools as a team would first write them, not against no tools at all. The four share one application, one set of domain functions, one data set, and one reset, and differ only in what one environment variable exposes, read at request time so a single production build serves all four.

V3 is deliberately thin, and says so. A V3 with a revision check and an approval page would be most of V4 written by hand, and the comparison would measure our wrapper against our SDK. The thin version is what the review asked for (tools that call the same handlers without state, affordances, handoff, or recovery), and its report names the one change (a revision on writes) that would have fixed the scenario it fails.

Scripted first, model-driven later. A scripted agent is the upper bound of what an interface allows a careful client to do, it is reproducible to the byte, it costs nothing, and it runs offline in CI time. A model-driven benchmark answers a different question (how often a real agent gets it right) and needs a budget, a fixed model version, transcripts, and enough runs for its variance; running one before the scripted harness existed would have mixed harness bugs into model results. So the model runner shares the scenarios and checks, refuses to start without explicit configuration, and has not been run. Every output says that scripted success is not evidence of agent performance.

Outcomes are checked against the application's state, never the agent's report. A test-only snapshot endpoint (only with PLAN_REVIEW_TEST_RESET=1) returns the plan and its whole history; success, incorrect mutations, and lost updates are computed from it. The one thing taken from the agent is the reason it relayed for an unavailable control, compared with the application's own sentence, because relaying the reason is the task.

Tokens are "n/a", not estimated. Bytes are measured and reported as bytes. Converting them to tokens would present an estimate in the same table as measurements, and the bytes a browser agent reads (an accessibility snapshot) and the bytes a tool-calling agent reads (JSON-RPC messages) are not the same input to a model anyway.

The ledger as the one history (Surface contract v0.9)

The ledger holds recorded changes and pre-handler refusals now, because an agent reads it as the history. An agent demoing the Plan Board over MCP reported two gaps: the revision "Approve March" moved had no entry, and its own stale edit, refused by the server's gate, was missing while <ns>.ledger said every refused act was in it. The contract had been precise ("the ledger records what reached act"), but an agent cannot tell a revision the application moved from one it missed, and "refused" in the description read as every refusal. Two ways out: make the description narrower, or make the ledger hold what an agent needs to account for every revision. We did the second and made the description exact: acts through the surface, changes the application recorded, and refusals the runtime made before the surface for a caller it admitted. Nothing else, so a caller the runtime refused for lack of credentials still leaves no trace on a protected surface ([S-AUTH-3]).

record does not bump. The application owns its change: it may keep its own revision (setRev, app mode), move it more than once, or move it inside a transaction the surface cannot see. A record that also moved the revision would move it twice in the first case and at the wrong moment in the others, and it would announce a change to onChange listeners that the application has not made yet. So the application changes state and moves the revision first, then records, passing the revision it read before as revBefore; the entry spans the move. For the same reason record runs no handler and takes no part in act ordering ([S-ACT-9]).

The provider hook in core, not a hook the integrator wires. The first design was a bridge.onResult to pass to createAXE({ onResult }). It would need the caller's identity (the hook context carries only onBehalfOf, and not for a site-key caller or a refusal before the runtime copied it), the envelope's input (for a domain action's entryId), and whether the handler ran (so a refusal the surface already ledgered, or a handler that threw, is not counted twice), none of which HookContext has; and a surface served without the wiring would keep the old gap while its ledger described itself as complete. The server already knows which provider supplied an action, so it now calls an optional ActionProvider.onResult with a ProviderResultContext carrying all four. The change is additive (an optional member, one call in the result path), addProvider is the only wiring, and a provider hook's type does not accept a HookContext, so it cannot be passed to createAXE by mistake and count twice (and at run time a call without handled, or a second call for one request, is ignored).

Relay (the optional remote integration path)

The broker is an optional SDK adapter, and it reuses the bridge. Browser-native WebMCP reaches a surface directly and is the package default. An agent outside that browser still needs a transport, so the relay's mirror implements the Surface interface domainActions reads (observe, ledger, get, entries, availability, currentRev, act), and a resolver returns the caller's tab's mirror. Tool definitions, the ladder, action events, MCP derivation, HTTP sessions, and OAuth are reused; the relay adds transport and identity mapping without becoming the state owner. The mirror refuses register and freeze: the page owns its entries. This separation also leaves room for a company-hosted remote service without putting its deployment burden on consuming developers.

One WebSocket from the page, ws on the server. A WebSocket is the one browser-native transport that carries requests both ways on one authenticated connection; SSE plus POST would need a second authenticated channel per act and correlation across them. Node has a WebSocket client from 22 but no server, and a hand-written server would be framing, masking, fragmentation, and limit code the SDK would have to keep secure. ws (8.x, about 150 kB unpacked, no dependencies) is a dependency of @summationai/axe-relay only; the browser client uses the platform's WebSocket and imports nothing at runtime.

Relay tokens are HS256 JWTs with sub and org. The first real integration will mint the token in its own backend with its own JWT code and a dedicated key, with { sub, org, mid, exp, aud }. A bespoke format would have forced it to use our helper; a JWT lets it use either, and the relay checks what matters: the algorithm (HS256 only), the signature, the audience, the expiry, and a lifetime of at most a day. The page presents the token in its first message, not in the URL, so it does not land in access logs.

The page is authoritative and the relay presents offset revisions. The page's surface.act decides every act, so its queue and checks apply. But a reloaded page starts a new surface at revision 0, and two tabs of one person count independently, so a raw revision read before a reload, or from another tab, could pass the check of a different state. The relay adds a random base per tab and an offset per page instance, translates expectedRev back before forwarding, and pins an agent to a tab from its first use; the ledger's sequence numbers continue the same way. Agents treat revisions as opaque, so the large numbers cost nothing.

Approval is a page-side gate, answered on the next identical call. A high-risk act could have blocked the tool call until the person decided, but the agent could not then tell the person what to approve, and MCP clients time out long calls. So the first call returns unavailable with approval_required and a sentence to say, the page shows Approve and Deny, and the next call with the same entry, text, and expectedRev runs once. The request is not a surface act, so it is not in the page's ledger; the act that runs after approval is. The gate lives in the page because only the page knows the person is there; its limit (a script in the page can press it) is documented. (Revised for unattended mode, below: when the person is not at the page, the tool call does block, because the question then goes to the person through the client rather than through the agent.)

Unattended is the default remote mode, and the tab it runs in is injected, not paired. When an agent outside the browser uses the optional remote path, the person signs in to the agent's own UI (MCP OAuth), a host (@summationai/axe-host) opens the application for them in a hidden browser session, easy mode derives the surface there, and the relay connects that tab. Nobody can read a pairing code from a hidden tab, and none is needed: the host mints the relay token for the person the session is for and sets window.__AXE_RELAY__ with an init script before the page runs. injectedRelay() reads the global at call time, never at import for server rendering.

In unattended mode the person approves in the agent's UI, in the same tool call. The panel's Approve assumes someone is looking at the page; in a hidden session no one is. MCP elicitation is the channel a person already sees: the client renders it, and the specification says the model cannot answer it. So when a tab that takes approvals from the agent holds an act, the relay asks on the calling tool call's own session and waits: a one-checkbox form for ordinary acts (with the act's text, unless sensitive), and URL mode to a relay-hosted approval page for sensitive acts or clients with URL mode only, since a form shows its content to the client and a page the relay serves does not. In-line was chosen over "return and retry" because it is one tool call with the decision in the middle, so the agent cannot garble or skip telling the person, and the retry cannot race a changed page; the tab still holds the decision bound to entry, op, text, and expectedRev, used once, so a cancelled call or a client without elicitation falls back to exactly the old retry path. A client with no elicitation gets approval_required with instructions and, where the relay serves approval pages, a link: never an act on the model's say-so, and never a decision from a tool argument.

The tab, not the relay, decides whether a relay may approve. A new message (approve / deny, relay to tab) carries the decision; the tab grants its gates exactly as its panel does (the relay gate and the surface's APPROVER, so an auto-derived gate is one decision too) and records it in its ledger with who decided and where (op: "approve", actor <principal> (approved in the agent's MCP client)). The tab accepts it only when it connected with approvals: "agent" or "both" (the unattended default), so an attended tab keeps its property that nothing but the person at the page approves, even against a compromised relay. The act itself is then re-sent and runs under the usual agent actor, so the ledger shows the decision and the act as two lines rather than overloading the actor.

The approval page establishes the person from their own session, not from the link. The link is single use, short-lived, and bound to one approval, principal, tenant, and request, but a link can leak (it is shown to the model in the fallback), so it is not a credential: approvals.identify(request) must name the same principal and tenant from the person's own session, the post needs the page's nonce and a same-origin Origin, and the page cannot be framed. Without identify the relay serves no page outside development and never offers URL mode.

Stop moves to the agent's side. With no indicator there is no Stop button, so relay_stop ends a session as Stop does (revoke, refuse, close with the Stop code so the host closes its context), relay.stop(who) serves a host's own watch page, and revoking the OAuth grant cuts the agent off entirely. Letting the agent stop is safe: stopping only ever removes access.

Development pairing uses a code the person reads from the tab. A development relay must be close to zero configuration and still not let any local web page or process drive a signed-in tab. It listens on loopback only, refuses a non-loopback peer or Host (DNS rebinding), serves development tokens only to allowed origins, requires a key on /mcp (stdio needs none), and binds an agent to a person only after it presents the code shown in that person's tab. The stdio form is the zero-configuration path for Claude Code; the HTTP form prints a claude mcp add command with the key.

Stop is for the page; leaving is not Stop. Stop revokes the token and marks the tab stopped, so every later act is refused with a reason the agent can relay. A reload is not Stop: the relay keeps the tab so an agent's work survives the person refreshing, and an act sent during the reload waits for the new page. rekey exists because the first integration switches tenants without a reload: it removes the old record and revokes the old token before connecting as the new identity, so nothing of one tenant's session reaches another's agent.

Easy mode: derived surfaces (Surface contract v0.9)

Derived is the base layer, not a separate product. A derived entry is an ordinary entry with a source marker on an ordinary surface, so the act queue, the revision guard, the ledger, freezes, the bridges, WebMCP, and expose apply unchanged, and declared entries stand beside derived ones in one table. The alternative, a parallel "page agent" API, would have forked every guarantee the contract already states.

Tiers are stated, because derived acts are weaker and must say so. A click cannot carry expectedRev into a server write. The surface re-reads the page before every act and refuses a stale one, which is real protection within the tab, but not a conditional write. Calling that out as the derived tier, and making a rule's handler the path to the declared tier without editing components, keeps the claim honest and the upgrade small.

Risk errs high, and unknown means high. The cost of a false high is a question to the person; the cost of a false low is an agent deleting something. So a control the heuristics do not recognize is high risk and needs approval by default, and coverage lists every one with a rule to paste. Running the scan over the reference application found the one mistake the opposite choice invites: "Freeze (pause agents, cancel their requests)" read as a low-risk "cancel". View and commit words now count only in the verb position; destructive words count anywhere.

Approval in the page is the person's call, not a token. An approval-gated entry reports a handoff with no url (there is no approval page to return from inside a tab); handle.approve(id) opens it for one act. The SDK cannot tell who calls approve, so the contract says it must only be wired to the person's own interaction. Server-side approval requests ([P-APPR-1]) remain the path for anything that must be bound to a principal and a tenant.

Keys come from what the person sees. Route, named containers, role, and accessible name survive re-renders and restructuring, and they are readable in a configuration file. The known failure modes (dynamic text, translation, duplicates) are documented with the fix (a data-surface-id or a rule's id), rather than hidden behind positional paths that break on every layout change.

The scan flushes before observe and act by wrapping them on the surface object. Coalescing DOM changes is necessary for performance, but an agent must never act on a revision the page has already moved past. Wrapping the two methods (and restoring them on stop) was the smallest change that guarantees it without adding a hook to the core surface.

Hidden controls are left out by default. The brief listed hidden as unavailable. On real pages hidden subtrees are closed tab panels, mobile duplicates of navigation, and unmounted menus; listing them doubled tables and produced duplicate names. They are skipped by default (hidden: "unavailable" restores the listing), while controls behind a modal, which the agent can reach by closing it, are listed as unavailable with the dialog named.

The auto code is a separate subpath, shared like the main entry. It adds about 55 kB minified (about 20 kB gzipped) to a page, over the surface core's 30 kB (12 kB gzipped), so it is not in @summationai/axe-surface; SurfaceProvider and autoActions import it at runtime (./auto.js) rather than inlining copies, as the hooks do with the main entry.

Integration (package first, remote by choice)

A codemod plus a prompt, not only a guide. The trials' integrations were written by hand from the docs, and each one spent most of its effort on the same mechanical steps: finding the root, choosing a gate, writing the provider, getting the install right for the package manager, and remembering expose only in development. A guide describes those steps; it cannot see the application, so every reader re-derives the root file and the flag from scratch, and an agent following it produces a different diff each time. axe surface init does the mechanical part deterministically: it reads the app, prints the diff before writing, touches only the mount line and two new files, follows the file's own style, and does nothing on a second run, so the change is reviewable in a minute and safe to re-run. What a codemod cannot do is judgment: which controls matter, the application's own words for a reason, which actions are destructive, which fields are private. That is the prompt's job, and the prompt is backed by llms.txt so the rules it applies are the same ones every other integration reads. The coverage report connects the two: it tells the agent what the codemod left open, in an order it can work through, and tells it again after each change. The guide stays as the reference for everything the codemod does, so nothing it writes is magic. The codemod edits text rather than an AST on purpose: one exact edit per framework, with a named manual step when the expected element is absent, is easier to trust than a transform that can rewrite anything, and it adds no parser to the CLI.

The default install has no standalone server. The surface registry, revision, approval gate, and ledger already live in the consuming page, so requiring a relay plus MCP server for every install duplicated deployment without adding authority. axe surface init now installs only @summationai/axe-surface and emits SurfaceProvider webMcp (or exposeWebMcp for plain pages). --remote adds the relay client; --relay and --relay-dev imply it. This preserves the original remote capability for Claude Code and other out-of-browser agents while making the dependency and operational boundary explicit. A later company-hosted service can implement that remote transport centrally and become a product moat without being a prerequisite for the browser-native package.

Reading the page and waiting (Surface contract v0.9, [S-AUTO-14] to [S-AUTO-16])

Content is read beside the controls, not as entries. The status of a project, a table of tasks, and a generated report are what the person reads, not what they act on. Registering them as entries would move the revision whenever a live page updated its text (the reason derived surfaces stopped bumping on table content) and would put thousands of rows into observe. A read is a separate, bounded query that returns the page as it stands, under the revision it stood at.

Sections by heading, with fallbacks, rather than a DOM dump or an accessibility tree. An agent asked "what is the status" needs "Status: At risk" next to its heading, not a tree of divs. Headings are what screen readers navigate by; where a page has none (the first target has no landmarks and titles its cards with styled divs), a dialog, a named region, a sectioning element, or a card whose first child is a title scopes a section, and content after the card returns to the section around it. Real headings are otherwise flat, as a screen reader reads them, because scoping every wrapper that starts with a heading misfiled the content after page headers.

Key-value pairs need a cue. Two short sibling elements are a pair only when one is marked as a label (a class, a label, a dt, a trailing colon) or the container is classed as a field; "Label: value" lines are fields outside a rich-text document and prose inside one. Without the cue, counters and badges ("3 items") became fields.

Charts are named, never read. A Highcharts chart with its accessibility module off still renders axis labels and numbers as SVG text. Reading them would hand an agent numbers without their meaning; the reader reports the chart's title and says its values cannot be read, and coverage lists it. A chart with an accessible name that states what it shows is read by that name, which is the fix coverage suggests.

Regions by name, selectors only from the configuration. An agent may ask for an entry, a landmark, a dialog, or a heading by the name it sees; a CSS selector is a reviewed part of the configuration (read.regions), so an agent cannot aim the reader at arbitrary markup, including markup the redaction rules were not written for.

Paging by characters of Markdown, with a cursor into a section. Agents' context is counted in text, so the bound is the size of the rendering the agent will read. A cursor names a section and an offset into its text (checked against the section's heading), so a long report is continued rather than cut, and a page that changed under the cursor says so and restarts.

read returns Markdown by default over MCP. It is about half the size of the structured form and is what an agent quotes; format: "sections" gives the structure to a program.

Waiting is mutation-driven and bounded, in the page. A wait checks after each batch of DOM mutations (coalesced), at least every pollMs, and exactly when an idle period could end; it never spins, is capped at two minutes, and ends when the surface stops. Waiting in the page, rather than polling observe from the agent, is what lets it see a toast that appears and disappears between two polls, and it keeps the agent's turn count low.

The reader travels on the surface under a symbol. The bridges and the relay's mirror find read and wait on any surface (CONTENT, a global symbol, as the approver is) without importing the derivation, so @summationai/axe-surface/axe stays a server module and a declared surface simply has no content actions available. The relay forwards both to the tab and translates revisions, as it does for acts.

The bundle bound moved. The reader and the waiter are about 26 kB minified (9.5 kB gzipped). A separate subpath would keep easy mode smaller, but reading and waiting are what let an agent answer from the page at all, and the bridges need them on the same handle, so they ship with it and the bound was raised to 120 kB (43 kB gzipped).

Unattended mode (the host)

A hosted headless browser, because the person should never have to open the site. The product decision was that the person authenticates in the agent's own UI and the agent acts on their behalf, through the UI, with no API layer. The relay alone needed a tab the person opened and kept open. The alternatives were an API beside the UI (rejected: it is the drift the SDK exists to avoid, and the first real target has stateful controls whose logic lives only in the page) or a browser-driving agent reading pixels and markup (rejected: no reasons, no revision, no approvals). Running the application's own page in a server-side browser keeps every guarantee the surface already gives: the page's handlers, availability, revision check, ledger, and easy-mode derivation are unchanged, and the relay carries the page to the agent exactly as for a person's tab. One Chromium with one context per identity is the smallest unit that isolates cookies and storage between people without paying a browser process each. Playwright is the most dependable way to drive Chromium from Node; playwright-core (no browser download) is a dependency of @summationai/axe-host only, the browser is installed or supplied where the host runs, and nothing reaches the application's pages or bundles.

No pairing is safe here because the host opens the tab. Pairing exists to prove that the tab an agent reaches belongs to the person the agent speaks for, when the tab and the agent met independently. In unattended mode the host starts the tab for the identity the agent's verified token names, mints that tab's relay token for the same identity, and injects it before any page script runs, only into the application's origin; the relay then serves the agent only tabs of that identity, as it always does. There is nothing left to prove, and a pairing code nobody can see would only fail. What pairing also bought (the person knows an agent is connected) moves to the agent's UI: the person started the conversation, approvals are asked there, and Stop is a request to the agent, the host's own control, or revoking the grant.

The SDK does not issue application sessions. A host that minted its own session for the app would become a second authentication system with the power to be anyone; one that forwarded the agent's OAuth token into the page would put a bearer token for another audience in a browser. The application already knows how to create a session for a user it has verified, so sessionFor asks it to, with the verified identity and token in hand, and returns cookies, headers, or storage the host only applies. Development uses a storage state an operator captured once (axe host login), labelled as exactly that.

Refused navigations answer 204. Aborting a blocked navigation commits an error page, which unloads the application and disconnects its surface; a 204 response to a navigation leaves the current document in place, so the page keeps running and the agent can observe again. Subresources are allowed by default because real applications load fonts, scripts, and identity-provider calls from elsewhere; restrict: "all" is there for those that do not, and an egress policy remains the operator's.

extraTools in @summationai/axe-mcp, and handleAgent on the relay. A screenshot is MCP image content, not an AXE result, and the relay's tools had to stay the derived ones (the ladder, idempotency, elicitation). The smallest general addition was a list of tools the embedding code answers itself; the host uses it for host_screenshot. handleAgent exposes the relay's own request path, tool-call context included, so approvals by elicitation work through the host exactly as through the relay's own MCP server.
